summary: Describes private SIP extensions that let a network of trusted servers assert the identity of authenticated users, including the P-Asserted-Identity header, and applies existing privacy mechanisms. It works only inside a domain with agreed policies and is not a general identity solution. It was later updated by RFCs 5876 and 8217.

plainLanguage.summary: In an ordinary phone network the operator knows who is calling and can pass that on for services such as caller return, while also letting people block their number. This document does the same for a closed SIP phone network by having trusted servers attach a verified identity to a call.

questions: how do trusted sip networks assert identity
what is the sip privacy id token
what is a sip trust domain
how does sip privacy for asserted identity work
subtitle: How a trusted phone style network can tell the other side who a caller really is, while still letting the caller stay private.

tldr.problem: Telephone providers running SIP needed to pass along the real, authenticated identity of a caller for services like call return and call trace, but baseline SIP has no trusted way to do that while also honoring a caller's wish to stay private.
tldr.mechanism: Trusted proxies insert a P-Asserted-Identity header holding the identity they verified, and strip it again before messages leave the Trust Domain when the caller asked for privacy with the Privacy header's id token.
tldr.outcome: A small header based mechanism let SIP networks emulate familiar calling identity delivery and blocking; RFC 3325 is Informational and limited to a single Trust Domain, and it was later updated by RFC 5876 and RFC 8217.

today: RFC 3325 is an Informational RFC and remains limited to use inside a single Trust Domain. It was later updated by RFC 5876 and RFC 8217.

sections.title: Why Asserted Identity Is Needed
sections.content:
Many providers chose SIP as the protocol for telephone service over IP networks. Their networks need a way for trusted elements, such as SIP proxy servers run by the provider, to communicate the identity of subscribers, and also to withhold that identity from parties that are not trusted when necessary. These networks generally assume some level of transitive trust among providers and the devices they run.

Such networks have to support traditional telephone services and meet regulatory and public safety needs, including delivery of calling identity, blocking of calling identity, and the ability to trace the originator of a call. Standard SIP can support each of these separately, but some combinations cannot work without the extensions in this document. For example, a caller who wants privacy and puts only limited information in the From header field cannot be identified by the recipient, so services such as call trace stop working.

The document offers a very limited, simple mechanism. It grew out of an earlier attempt to solve identity and privacy problems within a Trust Domain, and a more comprehensive cryptographic mechanism was under study by the SIP working group at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone-over-IP providers wanted the same calling features people expect from the ordinary phone network. Plain SIP could not combine privacy with a reliable record of who really called, so this extension was added.

sections.title: Trust Domains and Their Rules
sections.content:
The extensions only apply inside a Trust Domain, where users and end systems explicitly trust the nodes to publicly assert each party's identity and to withhold it outside the domain when privacy is requested. How the network works out the identity to assert is outside the scope of the document, though it usually involves some form of authentication. The document does not provide a general identity or privacy model for use between different trust domains or on the open Internet, and its assumptions about trust between user and network may not hold elsewhere.

A key requirement is that all nodes in a Trust Domain behave according to an agreed set of specifications called Spec(T). This set must state how users are authenticated, how communication between nodes and between user agents and nodes is secured, how hosts are determined to be part of the domain, the default privacy handling when no Privacy header is present, that the nodes comply with SIP and with this document, and the privacy handling for identity. The integrity of the mechanism depends on every node knowing, by configuration, that all the others will behave in the prescribed way.

The asserted identities are not cryptographically certified, so they can be forged, replayed or falsified in any architecture that does not meet the requirements. They also do not say which entity is asserting the identity, so the information is only meaningful when it is received securely from a node known to be a member of the Trust Domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme only works inside a closed group of servers that all follow the same written rules. Outside that group there is nothing to stop someone faking an identity, so the mechanism must not be used there.

sections.title: Proxy Behavior
sections.content:
The mechanism relies on a new header field called P-Asserted-Identity, which holds a URI, commonly a SIP URI, and an optional display name. A proxy that handles a message can, after authenticating the originating user in some way, insert the header and forward the message to other trusted proxies. A proxy about to forward a message to a proxy or user agent it does not trust must remove all P-Asserted-Identity values if the user requested privacy.

When a proxy receives a message from a node it does not trust and wishes to add the header, it must authenticate the originator and use the resulting identity. If the message comes from a node it trusts, it may use any P-Asserted-Identity value as if it had authenticated the user itself. If no such header is present, a proxy may add one containing at most one SIP or SIPS URI and at most one tel URL. A value must consist of exactly one address, and if there are two values one must be a SIP or SIPS URI and the other must be a tel URL.

On the way out, a proxy must first decide whether it trusts the next node. If it does, it leaves untouched any P-Asserted-Identity values it generated or received from a trusted source. If it does not trust the node, it must look at the Privacy header, if present, to see whether the user asked for the identity to be kept private. A user agent server behaves similarly: it must not use a P-Asserted-Identity value if the message came from an element it does not trust.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy is like a phone operator who checks your account, writes your real name on the call, and then tears that note off before the call leaves the company's network if you asked to stay private.

sections.title: Choosing an Identity and Asking for Privacy
sections.content:
A user might be reachable under several valid identities. A second header, P-Preferred-Identity, lets a user agent suggest which one the trusted proxy should assert. The user agent sends it only to trusted proxies and must not put it in a message sent anywhere else, because sending it to an untrusted node could leak the hinted identity. A proxy may treat the suggestion as a hint about which of several valid identities to assert; if the hint matches no valid identity it knows for that user, it can insert a header of its own or reject the request, for example with a 403 Forbidden. The proxy must remove the user supplied P-Preferred-Identity header before forwarding.

To request privacy, a user adds the id token to the Privacy header. When that token is present, proxies must remove all P-Asserted-Identity values before forwarding to untrusted elements. If the Privacy value is none, the proxy must not remove them. If there is no Privacy header and the proxy is forwarding to an untrusted element, the proxy may include the header or remove it, a policy choice the Trust Domain must state in Spec(T). It is recommended that the header not be removed unless local policy prevents it, because removal can break services that depend on asserted identity.

Because a user may request several kinds of privacy in one message, all requested types must appear in the Privacy header. The document notes that unless every user of the Trust Domain can use the privacy services, forwarding the asserted identity may reveal information the user never asked to reveal, so it is strongly recommended that all users have access to those services.
sections.plainLanguage: A caller can hint which of their several addresses to show, and can ask to stay private. The network decides what to do when the caller does not say, and the safe default is written into the shared rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism is only a partial treatment of identity and privacy in SIP. It gives end users no way to share identity information securely end to end without a trusted service provider. Identity information the user marks as private can be seen by any intermediary inside the Trust Domain, and it is protected only by transitive trust, which is no stronger than the weakest link in the chain.

The document also warns that the asserted identities are not certified, so they are subject to forgery, replay and falsification in architectures that do not meet the requirements, and that the asserted identity does not identify who is asserting it, so it is only meaningful when received securely from a known member of the Trust Domain.

The RFC requires that when a trusted entity sends a message to any destination carrying a party's identity in a P-Asserted-Identity header, the entity must take precautions to protect that identity from eavesdropping and interception, so that its confidentiality and integrity are preserved. Hop-by-hop security at the transport or network layer, such as TLS or IPsec with suitable cipher suites, can meet that requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the trusted group, a private identity is still visible to the operators, and the whole scheme is only as safe as its weakest server. Outside the group the identity can be faked, so it is only trustworthy when it arrives over a secured link from a known server.
